passage: The power went off at two, and the fan slowed to a stop. Five-year-old Francis kicked his blocks across the floor and burst into tears when his sister Harsha asked him to pick them up. Then he smacked her arm. Harsha almost shouted back. Instead she wet a towel, spread it on his neck, poured him a cup from the clay pot, and pulled the mat into the shady corridor. Ten minutes later Francis was humming, stacking blocks again.

qa.q: What did Harsha spread on Francis's neck?
qa.a: She spread a wet towel on his neck.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he kicked his blocks and hit Harsha?
qa.a: He felt hot, cross and tearful; the stifling afternoon after the fan stopped seems to have made him irritable rather than simply naughty.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: The heat was making Francis cranky; instead of scolding, Harsha cooled him with a wet towel, water and shade, and his mood changed quickly.

qa.q: What was it like for Harsha when Francis smacked her arm?
qa.a: It stung and she nearly shouted back, but she chose to look at the heat behind it and helped him cool down instead.

grounding: Shows a young child made irritable, tearful and quick to hit by stifling heat, and how cool water, shade and rest change his behaviour faster than correction.

passage: Harsha's cheeks were bright red when her father Darshan collected her from the school gate at noon. The auto stand was a long, sunny walk away. Halfway there, four-year-old Harsha dropped her bag, stamped her feet and whacked his leg. 'Harsha, no hitting!' Darshan began, then stopped. Her hair was soaked with sweat. He steered her into the shade of the bus shelter, let her drink from his steel bottle and splashed a little water on her wrists. She leaned against him, quiet. 'Better?' She nodded and picked up her bag.

qa.q: Where did Darshan take Harsha after she hit his leg?
qa.a: He steered her into the shade of the bus shelter.

qa.q: How was Harsha feeling on the long, sunny walk?
qa.a: She felt hot, cross and fed up; stamping and whacking her father's leg show the heat had shortened her temper.

qa.q: Which worked better, the scolding or the shade, and why?
qa.a: The shade, water and a rest worked: once Harsha cooled down she calmed and picked up her bag by herself.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the hit differently once he noticed her sweat-soaked hair?
qa.a: He could see it as a sign that she was overheated and uncomfortable, not plain naughtiness, so cooling her down made more sense than punishing.

grounding: Shows a young child turned irritable and quick to hit by midday heat, and a parent who finds shade and water work faster than correction.

passage: The heatwave had turned the playground in Zagreb into an oven. Hana, her cheeks blotchy red, snatched the spade from a smaller boy and whacked the sandpit. When her dad, Ivan, told her to say sorry, she burst into tears and yelled, 'I hate this park!' Ivan almost began a lecture. Instead he carried her into the shade of the chestnut tree, handed her his water bottle and dribbled some on her wrists. She drank in big gulps. Ten minutes later she gave the spade back on her own.

qa.q: Where did Ivan carry Hana?
qa.a: Into the shade of the chestnut tree.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when she yelled that she hated the park?
qa.a: She was hot, cross and miserable without knowing why; the heat had made her irritable and teary.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than a lecture, and why?
qa.a: Shade and water cooled Hana's body first, and then she returned the spade by herself.

qa.q: How might the smaller boy see Hana at that moment?
qa.a: He probably felt startled and upset, seeing only a bigger girl grabbing his spade, not the heat behind it.

grounding: A young child in stifling heat grabs, hits and cries, and shade and water change her behaviour faster than correction.

passage: By the last period, the fan in KG-B only pushed warm air around. Aditi, usually the first to share crayons, scribbled over her partner's drawing and kicked the bench. When Bidisha Miss asked why, her lip wobbled. 'I don't know!' Bidisha noticed her flushed face and dry lips. She took the whole class out to the shady verandah, handed out water and let them lie on mats with wet hankies on their foreheads. Soon Aditi curled up and whispered sorry to her partner.

qa.q: What did Bidisha notice about Aditi's face?
qa.a: Her flushed face and dry lips.

qa.q: Why did Aditi's lip wobble when she said 'I don't know'?
qa.a: She felt upset and confused; she was hot and cranky but didn't understand why she was acting that way.

qa.q: Why was moving the class to the verandah a wise choice?
qa.a: It dealt with the heat itself, with shade, water and rest, instead of only punishing the kicking.

qa.q: What was it like for Aditi's partner when the drawing was scribbled over?
qa.a: The partner may have felt hurt and surprised, since Aditi usually shares, until the whispered sorry.

grounding: A kindergarten child in a stifling classroom turns irritable without knowing why, and cooling and rest settle her.

passage:
Monday: Afternoon power cut in Nagpur. Arohi threw her doll at the wall and howled when her mother, Aparna, asked her to tidy up. Aparna scolded; Arohi cried harder and hit the cushion.
Wednesday: Same sticky heat. This time Aparna noticed Arohi's sweaty neck before the whining began. She filled a bucket, let Arohi splash her feet in the balcony shade and gave her lemon water.
Saturday: When Arohi snapped at her cousin, Aparna only said, 'Water and shade first, na?' Arohi went and sat by the bucket herself.

qa.q: What did Aparna give Arohi on Wednesday?
qa.a: A bucket to splash her feet in the balcony shade, and lemon water.

qa.q: How was Arohi feeling on Monday when she threw her doll?
qa.a: She was hot, frustrated and upset, and the scolding made her feel worse, so she cried harder.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Wednesday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Aparna spotted the heat signs early and cooled Arohi down instead of scolding, which calmed her before a meltdown.

qa.q: How might the cousin have seen Arohi's snapping on Saturday?
qa.a: The cousin may have felt hurt at first, then watched Arohi calm down once she sat by the water.

grounding: Over several days a mother learns that water and shade change her hot, cranky child's behaviour faster than scolding.

passage: The bus to Nani's village was an hour late, and the Jaipur bus stand was baking in the May heat. Salma had been whining for twenty minutes. When her cousin brushed her arm, she hit him and burst into tears. Jyoti, her mother, almost scolded. Then she noticed Salma's red cheeks and dry lips. She led her into the shade of the ticket office, gave her the water bottle and wet the end of her dupatta to wipe her face and neck. Salma drank, leaned against her and went quiet. A little later she said sorry to her cousin by herself.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti lead Salma?
qa.a: Into the shade of the ticket office.

qa.q: Why did Salma hit her cousin?
qa.a: She was hot, uncomfortable and irritable from the heat, without knowing why she felt so cross.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti's choice work better than scolding?
qa.a: Water, shade and a cool cloth fixed what was really bothering Salma, so her behaviour changed quickly.

qa.q: How might Salma's cousin have felt when she hit him?
qa.a: He was probably startled and hurt, since he had only brushed her arm.

grounding: Shows a young child made irritable and tearful by heat hitting out, and cool water, shade and rest changing her behaviour faster than correction.
